title: Cut the routine think, keep the time for the critical one
outcomes: Sets a time ceiling for routine moves and forced moves, and says what the ceiling frees up
Tells a forced move, an equal-choice move and a tempting-move position apart under time pressure
Stops a long think at the ceiling and plays the best candidate that passed the safety scan
Recognises the positions where shortening the think is the mistake

steps.text: This lesson builds on *The clock is a budget*, which taught the sums and the three kinds of position. Now you act on them. A **ceiling** is the most time you allow a kind of move. Our rule of thumb: forced move, about 2 seconds; several moves about equal, about 10 seconds. The time you save is banked for the positions that need it.

steps.prompt: A 10+0 game lasts 30 of your moves. Eighteen are routine, with a ceiling of 10 seconds each. You think 40 seconds on each instead. How many seconds beyond the ceiling do those 18 moves cost? Then: the 18 moves at 40 seconds use how many seconds more than your whole 600?

fields.label: Extra seconds spent on the 18 routine moves:
Seconds more than the 600 you start with (before increment, which this control lacks):

steps.text: **Answers:** (40 − 10) × 18 = 540 seconds. And 18 × 40 = 720, which is 120 more than 600. The flag falls before the critical moves arrive. A long think on a routine move is not free: it is paid for later from the moves that matter. Next: a position with several moves about equal. Decide how long it deserves.

steps.title: Where the ceiling helps, and where it does not
steps.prompt: Each position comes with 10 seconds as your ceiling for a routine move. Say what the position asks, then check.

steps.text: **Conditions.** The ceiling is for routine positions: nothing you could lose or win by force, several moves about equal. It fails when a capture, check or threat could win or lose material, or when a tempting move might have a hidden reply. Then run the *safety scan* (see *The safety scan: look before you move*) and think longer. At the ceiling, play the best candidate that passed the scan. The 2- and 10-second numbers are a first guess to test in your own games.

steps.prompt: Set your ceilings for your next timed game and write them down. Afterwards, list from memory your three longest thinks (the app does not record time per move yet, so this is a paper exercise) and say for each whether it was forced, equal-choice or critical. A long think on a routine move is what to cut.
